utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, could we have the case number that we have before us today? After that, we will have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-4-PT, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic (alias "Krkan"), Milojica Kos (alias "Krle"), Momcilo Gruban (alias "Ckalja"), Dusan Knezevic (alias "Duca") Zoran Zigic (alias "Ziga").

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we can now have the accused brought in, who will identify himself, and we will ask him who is representing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Milojica Kos, do you hear me? Can you hear me? Would you put your headset on, please, so you can understand the interpretation? Could we give a headset to the accused? This is his initial appearance, and he should understand what is going on. Do you hear me, Mr. Kos? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to ask you to tell us, since you are before the International Criminal Tribunal with two judges sitting, for reasons which are covered by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you will give us your name, your first name, your date and place of birth, as well as your profession and your current residence. After that, you may be seated. We are listening to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My name is Milojica Kos, born in 1963 in Lamovita, a village near Prijedor where I live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your profession, at least to the point of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We did not hear you. Would you please repeat your profession for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I now turn to the Office of the Prosecutor, represented by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. For the Prosecution, I am Michael Keegan, and I am assisted today by my colleague, Miss Ann Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Turning to the Defence, could we have the name and the bar to which the attorney is associated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Alexander Milne, I'm a member of the English bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we ask you to spell your name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: My surname is spelled M-I-L-N-E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Milne. We will now conduct the initial appearance, which is a significant part of our proceedings. You may be seated now. Mr. Kos, you may be seated. Mr. Kos, you are here before the International Criminal Tribunal in order to respond to the accusations which have been brought against you by the Prosecutor of the Tribunal under conditions that will be recalled shortly. We would recall that, according to the provisions in force, ever since the establishment of this International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, when an accused has been indicted, there must be a fundamental right which is respected. This is covered by Article 20 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. Article 20 was made clear and also corresponds to Article 21 which states that under a very quick period, the accused has the right to be informed of the charges against him, in a language that he understands, any charge or charges against him. After that, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence state, according to formality that we are going to respect, under Rule 62, it says that the -- which is called an initial appearance. First of all, we would like to turn to Mr. Milne and ask him whether the indictment has, in fact, been given to him and whether he verified that the accused understood its contents. After that, I will ask the same question of the accused. Mr. Milne?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I have had an opportunity to discuss it at length with Mr. Kos, and as I understand my instructions, he has read this at length and he is fully aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since this is the case, I will recall the indictment, and I myself, on behalf of my colleague, will ask the accused whether he understood the contents of the indictment today since this indictment has, in fact, been modified at the request of the Prosecutor. Before we have it read, we would like the Prosecutor to state what changes were made and what the changes are. We must be sure, both Judge Riad and myself, that between the time of the indictment that he was given and the indictment that will be read today, that there is no fundamental difference or at least that his counsel and himself are aware of what changes were made. I would first turn to the Prosecutor Mr. Keegan. The indictment was brought to my awareness a few moments ago, actually; that is, it was brought to the attention of the registry in the English version, which is a good thing for attorney, Mr. Milne, but it is rather difficult for the French-speaking attorney. However, we are not going to delay the initial appearance of the accused. So, Mr. Keegan, we will read the indictment. The registry has taken the English version. I think as regards -- formally, there is no problem, but I would like to be sure about what changes and what reasons for the changes there are so that things will be clear for both the accused and for his counsel. Mr. Keegan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. On the 28th of April of this year, the Prosecutor requested to withdraw certain named accused from the subject indictment, which had been confirmed on the 13th of February of 1995. On the 5th of May of this year, that request was granted, and subsequent to that order -- sorry, the 8th day of May -- that request was granted, and on the 12th of May of this year, we filed the notice of the withdrawal of the formerly named accused. This accused was arrested on the 28th of May of this year. There was, in fact, at the request of the registry, on that day a redacted version done for purposes of notification of the accused. There was a feeling, however, upon reflection, that that redaction had been too extreme in that it redacted not only the names of the accused but some of the content of the indictment. So today -- in fact, pursuant to review by myself -- a subsequent redacted version was issued. The changes from the original indictment, a copy of which I believe was given to the accused at the time of his arrest, so he would have had the full original indictment, the changes are as follows, Your Honour. First, in the cover page of the indictment, the first page, those formerly named accused, their names would be withdrawn from the caption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The names of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The names of the withdrawn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That you asked to have removed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mrs. Fauveau, you have an indictment with Mr. Kos's name and the names of the other co-accused who are under warrants of arrest and are being detained in the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We understand. Second modification?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Then on page 2 of the original indictment in paragraph 3, the word "guards" was deleted from that paragraph, and in the current redacted version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Why is that? I would like things to be very clear for the Defence here. The word "guards" was removed. You have to be clear, Mr. Keegan. I suppose it is because -- I mean, this is not my Trial Chamber that confirmed this -- but I suppose it is because the accused, against which charges are not being followed up on, were guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and none of the remaining accused are guards, so the term was now inappropriate. In the modified -- redacted version, I should say, it is now just reflected as "Text Deleted." That text was the word "guards." Then on the following page, page 3, paragraph 7 was deleted because that original paragraph 7 named those guards who have now been withdrawn from the indictment; and in the redacted version, number 7 still exists and it now reads, "Omitted accused withdrawn from the indictment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am working on the French version here; that's why I have to ask you these questions. But proceed, please. Thank you. Would you continue with your explanation because it makes it much clearer for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Then in the next paragraph, paragraph 8, three of the formerly named accused have been removed. They were reflected in that paragraph as letters A, B, and D; and in the now redacted version, you have only two of the remaining named accused, letters C and E from the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: C and E. Yes, all right. Only C and E are left. Keep this for a moment, Registrar. I can work here with Judge Riad. Yes, we agree. All right. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, we flip to page 10 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Paragraph 10, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, page 10, it would be paragraph 23 of the original indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. What are the changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And there in the caption, "Accused," which is now page 9 of the redacted indictment, two names were deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could I have the paragraph numbers, please? It makes it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 23, Your Honour, 23.1, and it's the caption just above that. You will see in the redacted version "Names deleted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And two names from the original indictment were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. They've been deleted. Yes, we agree. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we turn the page on the original to page 11 and go to paragraph 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- again, you have names of the two, same two accused withdrawn, and then the new indictment, the redacted version, I should say, you will see the phrase "Names deleted," and that reflects the same two accused who were withdrawn from the caption that we have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mrs. Fauveau, could you show me the version that you have in front of you, please? I don't want these names of people who are no longer accused to be called out. Very well. Is the Defence following this? Mr. Milne, do you follow it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the copy that I've been given does not have the section that my friend has just referred to. I suspect, although the copy I have is the most up to date, it's not the same as my friend's copy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. I've been endeavouring to follow this, and it's clear that the alterations don't have an immediate bearing upon Mr. Kos, in that many of the alterations refer to persons other than Mr. Kos. But the copy that I was given today and the copy that I was given last week are at odds with this; and therefore, if my learned friend has a copy that is the redacted version, as he's described it, it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have one available right now, Your Honour. As I indicated on Friday, a redacted version was prepared on short notice -- Friday night, actually -- and upon review, it was determined that too much had been redacted, and today we issued another redacted version to supersede the one issued on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Keegan, this is a public hearing. Without turning to the Defence, "I cancelled -- we took things out," "We added them", "We took too much out." This is not a supermarket here. These are very serious issues that we are dealing with here, and I want things to be very clear. You have modified it -- that is your right -- but it is the Defence's right to be brought up to date about what charges are being made. If you say that too much has been taken out, I can't simply accept that sentence. This is a sentence which is really that you would find in a flea market. "Too much." What do you mean, "Took out too much"? I suppose by that you mean that the charges against Mr. Kos need to be supported by other charges that are older and which you took out in favour of the withdrawal of the indictment. I want all this to be noted in the transcript. Is that what you're saying, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. As we get to the remaining redactions, I will indicate where we took out material on Friday that should have remained. I will indicate what those changes are, between the two redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. This has to be pointed out to the judges but it also has to be indicated to the Defence. Very well. All right. Let's go back to 24.1. 24.1. All right. Proceed, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In 24.1 then the names of two of the formerly charged individuals were deleted because they were two of the individuals for which a withdrawal was approved, and they were taken out of 24.1. They are the same two named accused who appear in the caption above, paragraph 23, because it's a series of charges that had been related to the same individuals. And then in the charges which follow, paragraphs 24.2 through 24.3, those same two names are redacted from each of the charges, so what remains is the two named accused which still exist on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Mrs. Fauveau, are you following this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, paragraph 25, the caption immediately above it, "Accused," the name has been deleted as that was one of the individuals for whom withdrawal had been approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The version that my colleague has is up to date. Very well. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 25.1, again the name of the individual has been removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And paragraphs 25.2 through 25.4, which are the charges following that, for that individual, have been deleted, redacted. And, Your Honour, this is a change from the redacted version from Friday. This is one of the individual crimes which were inadvertently or mistakenly deleted as they do form a basis for the charges relevant to this accused. What we have done is re-inserted the factual language of the charge but have not inserted the actual charges because they relate to that particular individual who was formerly named in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we then proceed to paragraph 26, it's the same format, Your Honour; that is, the name of the individual and the caption has been deleted. His name has been deleted from paragraph 26.1. And then paragraphs 26.2 to 26.4 again have been deleted as those are the charges which related to that formerly indicted individual. But the factual material relevant to that charge remains now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You are keeping the significant points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. For paragraph 27, again it's the same format. In the caption above it, the name "Accused" have been deleted, and there were four; and in the subsequent paragraph 27.1, the four names have been deleted, but the factual basis of the charge remains; and then paragraphs 27.2 to 27.4, the actual charges that were alleged against those four names accused have been deleted. Paragraph 28 follows the same format, and the caption and name of the formerly indicted accused has been deleted. His name has been deleted in two places from paragraph 28.1. And then the charges relating to that individual, paragraphs 28.2 to 28.4, have been deleted. Paragraph 29, similarly, the name has been deleted. Again, in paragraph 29.1, the name has been deleted. And paragraphs 29.2 to 29.4, the charges relating to that individual have also been deleted. For paragraph 30, the name of the individual has been deleted from the caption, the name of the individual has been deleted from paragraph 30.1, and then the charges which were in paragraphs 30.2 to 30.4 have been deleted. Paragraph 31 remains as it was in the original, as that individual is still a named accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Milne, did you follow what was said on the version that you were given?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. I think it's clear now. We will now ask the registrar to read the indictment on the basis of what has just been stated by the Prosecutor and which has been followed by both the Defence and by the judges. Mr. Kos, you have heard the indictment, you know that it has been changed based on things that have been explained to you, but now, before I ask you to plead guilty or not guilty to each of the counts, I would like the registrar to read the indictment. When you read the charge, we will ask Mr. Kos to rise and to state whether he pleads guilty or not guilty to each of the counts, which will avoid repetitions later on. That is, if the Defence agrees with our proceeding in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly we would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Mrs. Fauveau, you will read the indictment. When you get to Count 1, you will speak more slowly so that Mr. Kos can hear what you are saying, and I will ask the accused to rise and to think about what he's going to say, to state that he understands and whether he pleads guilty or not guilty. Remain seated for the time being. Mrs. Fauveau, would you begin to read the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The indictment. The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia -- Richard Goldstone, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia charges: 1. From about the 25th of May to about the 30th of August, 1992, Serb forces collected and confined more than 3.000 Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the opstina of Prijedor, Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the former Yugoslavia, in inhumane conditions, under armed guard, in the Omarska "camp" located in a former mining complex approximately fifteen kilometres from the town of Prijedor. As set forth below, the Serb forces killed, raped, sexually assaulted, beat and otherwise mistreated the prisoners at Omarska. 2. In May 1992, intensive shelling of Muslim areas in the opstina Prijedor caused the Muslim residents to flee their homes. The majority of them then surrendered or were captured by Serb forces. As the Serb forces rounded up the Muslims and any Croat residents, they forced them to march in columns bound for one or another of the prison camps that the Serbs had established in the opstina. The Serb forces pulled many of the Muslims and Croats from the columns and shot or beat them on the spot. On or about 25 May, 1992, about three weeks after Serbs forcibly took control of government authority in the municipality and two days after the start of large scale military attacks on Muslim population centres, Serb forces began taking prisoners to the Omarska camp. During the next several weeks, the Serb forces continued to round up Muslims and Croats from Kozarac, Prijedor town and other places in the municipality and interned them in the camps. Many of Prijedor's Muslim and Croat intellectuals, professional and political leaders were sent to Omarska. There were approximately 40 women in the camp and all the other prisoners in the camp were men. Within the area of the Omarska mining complex that was used for the camp, the camp authorities generally confined the prisoners in three different buildings: The administration building where interrogations took place and most of the women were confined; the garage or hangar building; the "white house," a small building where particularly severe beatings were administered; and on a cement courtyard area between the buildings known as the "pista." There was another small building known as the "red house" where prisoners were sometimes taken but most often did not emerge alive. Living conditions at Omarska were brutal. Prisoners were crowded together with little or no facilities for personal hygiene. They were fed starvation rations once a day and given only three minutes to get into the canteen area, eat and get out. The little water they received was ordinarily foul. Prisoners had no changes of clothing and no bedding. They received no medical care. Severe beatings were commonplace. The camp guards, and others who came to the camp and physically abused the prisoners, used all manner of weapons during these beatings including wooden batons, metal rods and tools, lengths of thick industrial cable that had metal balls affixed to the end, rifle butts and knives. Both female and male prisoners were beaten, tortured, raped sexually assaulted and humiliated. In addition to regular beatings and abuse, there were incidents of multiple killings and special terror. Many, whose identities are known and unknown, did not survive the camp. The persons accused in this indictment were commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we can't say guards. It's not guards. I think that's what has been taken out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And others responsible for the conditions and mistreatment of prisoners in Omarska camp or otherwise assisted the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic also known as "Mejakic" or "Meagic" was in charge of Omarska camp beginning in late June 1992 and was in a position of superior authority to everyone else in the camp. Before he took command of the camp, he was chief of security and had full authority over all the guards and any visitors. Before the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was a police official in Omarska village. Miroslav Kvocka and Dragoljub Prcac were deputies to Zeljko Meakic and were in positions of authority superior to everyone in the camp other than Meakic. For most of the first month of the camp's operation, Kvocka was the commander of the camp. Prior to the start of the war, both Kvocka and Prcac were officials at the Ministry of the Interior in Prijedor. Mladen Radic, also known as "Mlado Radic" or "Krkan," Milojica Kos, also known as "Krle" and Momcilo Gruban, also known as "Ckalja" were shift commanders who each supervised one of the three shifts of guards that operated the camp. As shift commanders when they were on duty, they were in positions of superior authority to all the camp personnel, second only to the camp commander and his deputies. In addition to the above-listed accused, who regularly performed duties in Omarska camp, other Serbs entered the camp subject to the authority of Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka and Dragoljub Prcac, where they killed, beat or otherwise physically abused prisoners. Among those who entered the camp were the following accused: Dusan Knezevic, also known as "Duca" and Zoran Zigic, also known as "Ziga." At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All acts or omissions set forth as grave breaches recognised by Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal occurred during that armed conflict and partial occupation. All of the prisoners at the Omarska camp and the Bosnian Muslims and Croats of the municipality of Prijedor referred to in this indictment were, at all relevant times, persons protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949. All of the accused in this indictment were required to abide by the mandate of the laws and customs governing the conduct of war including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Unless otherwise set forth below, all acts and omissions set forth in this indictment took place between 24 May and 30 August 1992. In each paragraph charging torture, the acts were committed by or at the instigation of, or with the consent or acquiescence of an official or person acting in an official capacity and for one or more of the following purposes: To obtain information or a confession from the victim or a third person; to punish the victim for an act the victim or a third person committed or was suspected of having committed; to intimidate or coerce the victim or a third person; and/or for any reason based upon discrimination of any kind. In each paragraph charging crimes against humanity, a crime recognised by Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the alleged acts or omissions were part of a widespread or large-scale or systematic attack directed against the civilian population, specifically the Muslim and Croat population of the Prijedor municipality. Paragraphs 4 through 15 are realleged and incorporated into each of the charges described below. The term "Serb" refers either to Bosnian citizens of Serbian descent or to individuals for whom it is unknown whether they were Bosnian Serbs or citizens of Serbia proper. Paragraphs 18.1 to 18.3 refer exclusively to the accused Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, at this point on, the charges -- well, would you prefer that we go about this in a different way? I turn to the Defence. In light of all of these changes, perhaps you will complete the reading of the indictment, and then I will go back to each of the counts. I wanted to simplify things, but when we look at all of these modifications, the legal officer of the Chamber suggested that we proceed differently. The registrar will continue to read and I will ask the accused to plead guilty or not guilty only later during this appearance. Continue, please, Mrs. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With respect to the allegations in this indictment, Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban knew or had reasons to know that persons in positions of subordinate authority to them at Omarska camp were about to commit those acts or had already committed those acts and failed to take the necessary and reasonable steps to prevent those acts or to punish the perpetrators after the acts had been committed. During the operation of Omarska camp, camp guards and others who were subordinate to Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban regularly and openly killed, raped, tortured, beat and otherwise subjected prisoners to conditions of constant humiliation, degradation and fear of death. The accused Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban in their capacity as superiors. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the wilful killing of Omarska prisoners including those described in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, herein after "Grave breaches" recognised by Articles 2(a) and 7(3) of the Statue of the Tribunal or; Alternatively, Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the murder of Omarska prisoners including those described in paragraphs hereunder, violations of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the murder of Omarska prisoners including those described in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity recognised by Articles 5(a) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the torture of Omarska prisoners, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2(b) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal or; Alternatively, Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the torture of Omarska prisoners, violations of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the torture of Omarska prisoners, crimes against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(f) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the rape of Omarska prisoners including those described in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity recognised by Articles 5(g) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in wilfully causing great suffering to Omarska prisoners, including those described in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal or; Alternatively, Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the commission of outrageous upon personal dignity, including humiliating and degrading treatment of the Omarska prisoners, violations of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(c) of the Geneva Conventions. Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in the unlawful confinement of civilians, including those listed in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2(g) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka, Dragoljub Prcac, Mladen Radic, Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban are criminally responsible for their own acts or omissions and for the acts of their subordinates in the unlawful imprisonment of the prisoners of Omarska, including those listed in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(e) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Paragraphs 20.1 up to 22.16 apply to the accused Meakic and Radic. Paragraph 23.1: The accused Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic and a third unknown person and others whose names have been deleted: In about July 1992, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic and a third unknown person savagely beat Becir Medunjanin on two occasions over a two-day period in the "white house." The accused assaulted Becir Medunjanin with a club, a chair, a baton and kicked him. The morning after the second assault, Becir Medunjanin died in the room and his body was removed from the camp immediately. Zoran Zigic and Dusan Knezevic participated in the wilful killing of Becir Medunjanin, a grave breach recognised by the Article 2(a) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Zoran Zigic and Dusan Knezevic participated in the murder of Becir Medunjanin, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zoran Zigic and Dusan Knezevic participated in the murder of Becir Medunjanin, a crime against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(a) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. 24.1: On or about 10 June 1992, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic went to the Omarska camp. Zigic, Knezevic were not regular guards at the camp but were allowed into the camp to murder, beat or otherwise physically abuse the prisoners. On that particular day, they called four prisoners at the Omarska camp, Emir Beganovic, Rezak Hukanovic, Asef Kapetanovic and Sefik Terzic into the "white house" and severely beat them. The accused used metal batons and cables, a knife, their fists and kicked the victims with their military-style boots. Victim Emir Beganovic: Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in the wilfully causing serious injury to the body or health of Emir Beganovic, a grave breach recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Emir Beganovic to cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Emir Beganovic to inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, recognised by the Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Victim Rezak Hukanovic: Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in wilfully causing serious injury to the body or health of Rezak Hukanovic, a grave breach recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Rezak Hukanovic to cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Rezak Hukanovic to inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Victim Asef Kapetanovic: Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in wilfully causing serious injury to the body or health of Asef Kapetanovic, a grave breach, recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Asef Kapetanovic to cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Asef Kapetanovic to inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Victim Sefik Terzic: Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in wilfully causing serious injury to the body or health of Sefik Terzic, a grave breach recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Sefik Terzic to cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Zoran Zigic, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting Sefik Terzic to inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. 25.1: Between early June and 3 August 1992, a guard at the Omarska camp who was a member of Mladen Radic's shift repeatedly forced "F" from a room where she was sleeping, took her to another room on the first floor of the administration building in the Omarska camp and subjected her to forcible sexual intercourse. Paragraph 26.1: Between early June and 3 August 1992, a guard at the Omarska camp forced "F" from the room where she was sleeping, took her to another room on the first floor of the administration building in the Omarska camp and subjected her to forcible sexual intercourse. Paragraph 27.1: Around 6 July 1992, on the pista, the victim Rizah Hadzalic, in response to a comment by a guard, used a common polite Bosnian Muslim expression "Bujrum." The accused, together with co-accused and a guard known only as Nedo went to Rizah Hadzalic and beat him for using this Muslim expression. The four accused and Nedo beat Rizah Hadzalic until he fell to the ground in a sitting position. About half an hour later, Rizah Hadzalic died as a result of the beating. Paragraph 28.1: In early June 1992, a large group of prisoners were confined in the canteen area of the administration building of the Omarska camp. One night an elderly man named Mehmedalija Nasic stood up and shouted in apparent protest over the prisoners' confinement. He was at the time distressed and possibly mentally disturbed by the conditions that he had been forced to endure. One of the guards at the Omarska camp ordered him to sit down. Nasic did not sit down and after a few minutes, a guard fired his rifle killing the victim and wounding several other prisoners sitting nearby. Paragraph 29.1: On or about 17 June 1992, a guard at the Omarska camp with four other guards whose names are not known took Serif Velic, a prisoner in the camp, to a room in the administration building where they stripped him to his underwear, kicked him in the testicles, repeatedly beat him with a baton and a rifle, and kicked him in the ribs, causing him to lapse in and out of consciousness. Paragraph 30.1: "F" was taken to the Omarska camp as a prisoner in early June 1992. Sometime between early June and 3 August 1992, "F" was taken to the Separcija building at the entrance to the Omarska camp and placed in a room where a former accused subjected "F" to forcible sexual intercourse. Paragraph 31.1: Around the latter part of June or first part of July 1992, near the building known as the "white house," a group of Serbs from outside the camp, including Dusan Knezevic, ordered prisoners, whose names are not known, to drink water like animals from puddles on the ground, jumped on their backs and beat them until they were unable to move. As the victims were removed in a wheelbarrow, one of the Serbs discharged the contents of a fire extinguisher into the mouth of one of the victims. Dusan Knezevic participated in wilfully causing a group of Omarska prisoners, whose names are not known, great suffering or serious injury to body or health, a grave breach recognised by Articles 2(c) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, or; Alternatively, Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting these unknown Omarska prisoners to cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. Dusan Knezevic participated in subjecting these unknown Omarska prisoners to inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, recognised by Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it signed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Signed, Richard J. Goldstone, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have the date?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This was confirmed on the 13th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, for the transcript we can say that it was modified at the time of the rest on the 28th of May, Friday, and again modified today under those conditions that were explained during these hearings and are noted in the transcript. Now, Mr. Kos, we're going to ask you to rise. First of all, did you hear this indictment and understand the sense of the modifications that were made? Both those are formal things because they have to do with withdrawals of accusations against some of the co-accused. In your own language, did you understand what was read to you? Was it translated to you in your own language? I would like you to confirm that to us first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now go to each of the counts, Mrs. Fauveau. We will go to the charges, and as each one is read out, we will ask you whether you plead guilty or whether you plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think we must begin with paragraph 19(3) which has the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You will read both of them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic, Miroslav Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just read the count, please, because we aren't going to read the entire indictment again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 recognised by Articles 2(a) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal or violations of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What count is that, please? Is that Count 1? Mr. Kos is here. How many counts does he have? I think there are 11 that concern Mr. Kos directly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are 12 counts that apply to Mr. Kos, and they are contained in paragraphs 19.3 to 19.13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But those paragraphs have been read. Now I should like you to isolate from that Count 1 without repeating the paragraphs. So Count 1, Mr. Kos is going to hear it such as it is specified in the indictment and as it has been juridically expressed by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 1 contained in paragraph 19.3, that is, acts of subordinates who participated in the wilful killing of Omarska prisoners, including those described in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, recognised by Articles 2A and 7(3) of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kos, do you plead guilty or not guilty to Count 1 of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, this count has been presented in a different way, but we will see what is the evidence, and will you please read the alternative count which corresponds to paragraph 19.4?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is for the same acts as 19.3, violations of the laws and customs of war, recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 3. This is contained in paragraph 19.5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They are acts of subordinates participating in the murder of Omarska prisoners, including those described in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity recognised by Articles 5A and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count 4, which is contained in paragraph 19.6.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually, it is a count contained in 19.6 and 19.7 which set out alternatively the acts of subordinates who participated in the torture of Omarska prisoners, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2B and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty, Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are the same acts as in paragraph 19.6, but this time these are violations of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 6 which corresponds to paragraph 19.8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are acts of subordinates who participated in the torture of Omarska prisoners, crimes against humanity, recognised by Articles 5F and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty? You have heard what's been interpreted for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Count number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a count contained in paragraph 19.9, acts of subordinates who participated in the rape of Omarska prisoners, including those described in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity, recognised by Articles 5G and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 8, which corresponds to paragraph 19.10.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The count contained in 19.10 and 19.11 are also put alternatively. These are acts of subordinates who participated in wilfully causing great suffering to Omarska prisoners, including those described in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2C and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count 9, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are the same acts as in paragraph 19.10, but this time qualified as violations of the laws or customs of war recognised by Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, and Article 3(1)(c) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 10, paragraph 19.12.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 19.12 refers to acts of subordinates who participated in the unlawful confinement of civilians, including those listed in paragraphs hereunder, grave breaches recognised by Articles 2G and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Count number 11. That corresponds to paragraph 19.13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is criminal responsibility for their own acts or omissions and for the acts of subordinates who participated in the unlawful imprisonment of prisoners of Omarska, including those listed in paragraphs hereunder, crimes against humanity, recognised by Articles 5E and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I had stopped at 11, but you said that there were 12 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, no, there are 11. There are 11 charges. Not 12, no, 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Prosecutor, 11 charges, 11 counts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kos, you may be seated. I will ask the registrar to note the plea of not guilty to all 11 counts that have been brought against you by the Prosecutor in the indictment which has just been read and which has been understood and heard in his own language, as read by the registrar. Now I would like to turn to the parties. This is the last phase of the initial appearance that has to do with the conduct of the future work. Turning to the Prosecutor, you know our Rules, but perhaps your colleague is less familiar with them. You know that from this point on, you must give a copy of any attachments, of the supporting material, that affect the accused or any witness statements. Where are you as regards that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are in the process of segregating the material that relates to this accused from the material which supported the original indictment, and we should be able to have that, provide it to the Defence within the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you note that, Mrs. Fauveau? It will be within a week. Today is the 2nd of June. So on the 9th of June, the accused and the Defence should receive everything that was attached to the indictment at the time of the indictment and any other statements that may have been made. All documents that are covered by 66, all documents 66, will you be able to produce them also within the same time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, the documents which apply to 66A(i), yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would ask like to recall that the 60-day time period, Mr. Milne, that there is 60 days starting from the request for filing of any preliminary motions as indicated in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like you to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me also remind you, Mr. Milne, the Rules have recently changed and now this is more favourable to -- it has to do not with the date of the initial appearance but the date that the materials were disclosed. I would like to ask the Prosecutor to understand that in this Trial Chamber, there is a legal officer who is a professional, that is Mr. Olivier Fourmy, who will be the person you can speak to, both of you, and that there will be a Pre-Trial Judge, because in the modification of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that are now being adopted and which will be adopted in a few weeks, it has been provided that a special judge who has been assigned to the status of the case will be assigned so that they will respect it. Mr. Keegan, what is the timetable that you have in mind for this case? I know perhaps this is also related to the co-accused, but what can you tell Judge Riad and myself today about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are in the process right now of preparing an amended indictment which will join this accused with the other three accused who are currently before this Chamber; that is the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic, into a consolidated indictment which will name all four, and we would hope to submit that for your consideration pursuant to Rule 50 very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, I don't think that it is not premature to set up a schedule today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Milne does know how this Tribunal operates, but do not hesitate to address any questions to Mr. Fourmy if you think they are necessary. So that there can be a proper link with the Office of the Prosecutor in this Tribunal, and this is the very sense of the changes within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that I am not going to indicate until they have been officially produced in both languages, but the very profound sense of this Tribunal is that one must attempt to start the trial as quickly as possible, and this is why the judges have taken and will take -- will not take more stringent initiatives than they did in the past. I would like you to have not only confidence in the legal office of the Tribunal in whom the judges do have their own confidence, but he is a professional judge and he will be in a position to allow both the Defence and the Prosecution to work together. I think that we can go even further once the indictment has been properly set up in respect of the other accused, and if this case still is placed before this Tribunal -- there are points of agreement or not disagreement, for the time being, I think that would be a bit premature. Mr. Milne, are there any comments that you would like to make or any questions that you would like to ask of the judges right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILNE
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Keegan, have you any questions you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, do you wish to make a statement? After that, you will be caught up within the trial. But today, in this initial appearance before the judges, this is the tradition of this Trial Chamber: We authorise you to make a statement, if you have something you wish to say about your detention conditions or about anything else. Succinctly, please. Or perhaps you have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have faith in justice and God. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fourmy, do you have any questions, any additional questions you would like to ask before we leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Registrar, I will ask you to ensure that even before the indictment has been modified, I would like us to have a, if you like, clean version of the indictment, the one that was read today. I would like to thank the registrar who was forced to perform all sorts of mental gymnastics -- we want to speak about the French-speaking judges -- who have agreed to work with an English version. The English attorney will understand the sensitivity that we have for the different countries. But we would like at least what was read today to have been in French and in English independent of any modifications of the indictments relating to the other accused. The final word is the judges. I turn to my colleague to ask if he has any points that he would like to clarify or any questions he would like to ask. Since no one has any further questions, I would say that the court will stand adjourned now that this initial appearance has been conducted.
